title: Yang Chu's Garden of Pleasure
dateDisplay: c. 4th–3rd centuries BCE, as transmitted in the Liezi
attributionNote: The chapters present the teaching of Yang Zhu (c. 440–360 BCE), whom Mencius attacked for refusing to sacrifice a hair of his body for the world. The text itself is the seventh book of the Liezi, compiled centuries later by followers; it is not a surviving work of Yang Zhu's own hand.
description: Yang Chu's Garden of Pleasure is the Liezi's book on the individual life: the vanity of fame, the brevity of consciousness, death as the great leveller, false virtue, duty to the living and the dead, the art of life, the happy voluptuaries, the joys of Tuan-mu Shu and the folly of craving long life. Its hedonism is not licence but a consistent refusal to trade the present for reputation or for an imaginary future, and it preserves one of the sharpest alternatives to the Confucian and Mohist ethics of its time.
historicalContext: Yang Zhu's position is known chiefly from his critics, Mencius above all; the Liezi chapter is the fullest surviving statement attributed to him, though its date and fidelity are disputed. Lionel Giles translated it for the Wisdom of the East series in 1912 as a companion to his Lieh-Tzü selection.
availabilityNote: Complete. All nineteen chapters of Giles's translation are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one chapter per page. The volume's introduction and contents are not part of the work.
